subject: Very slow processing last step using -I 100

messages.author: 08561d9df544eba2
messages.subject: Very slow processing last step using -I 100
parts:
I'm having an issue where the final reassembly step of subindel (I think) is taking quite a long time. After about 15 min. to align ~7 million paired end reads using -I 100 option, it begins "Processing .//core-temp-sum-07...@chrI-0000.bin". This step takes hours to go through the chromosomes (12 .bin files). I'm wondering if this is normal behavior, if there is any way to speed it up (upping process resource limits with ulimit or threads with -T option doesn't seem to do anything), or if there's some other kind of problem I'm having. 

Thanks!

-dylan

messages.author: 08561d9df544eba2
messages.subject: Re: Very slow processing last step using -I 100
parts: Since I didn't need the reassembly file, I was ignoring it, but I figured I'd take a look at it. I'm not sure it's supposed to look like this - it's thousands of individual fasta entries, each representing short stretches of the given chromosomes. Is this normal? It looks nothing like a normal genome.fa file you would get from some annotation (i.e. a few large entries for chromosomes).

messages.author: bce99ba71cd48eea
messages.subject: Re: Very slow processing last step using -I 100
parts:
Hi Dylan,

The "-I 100" option turned on the read re-assembly step in the Subread aligner for detecting long insertions and deletions (16bp or longer), and this step is relatively slower. A 3-5 hour running time is pretty normal when processing a high-coverage data set (like ~15 millions of reads from an RNA-seq sample). Also, we haven't make this step multi-threaded, hence it only runs on one CPU. You can avoid the read re-assembly step by specifying an "-I" option less than 16, or ignore this option.

The FASTA file contains the read assemblies where one or more indels were detected. General read assemblies from Subread are several hundred bases long, hence you have thousands of them. If you look at the name fields in the FASTA file, you can find the start location and the end location of this assembly on the chromosome, and also a CIGAR-formatted string for indicating the locations of indels detected in this assembly.

Cheers,
Yang
